text:
Recent research supports separating intent coverage from item dissimilarity: recommendations can look different while serving the same purpose. [Beyond Item Dissimilarities (2024/2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12327) demonstrates intent-based diversification. Recommendation-specific judge research also finds that richer metadata and longer histories improve agreement with human relevance judgments, though this does not establish reliability for sparse Amazon descriptions or twenty users. [From IR to RecSys (2025/2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.23312).

A practical rubric, inferred from these findings, should require supporting title/description spans for each judgment: redundant function, documented added capability, recent-history relevance, broad historical relevance, or insufficient evidence. Score these dimensions separately; textual similarity alone cannot establish duplication, and recent interactions cannot establish current intent with certainty. Mark compatibility, mood, and simulator diversity/conformity traits unknown unless explicitly supported by permitted evidence. [AbstentionBench (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038) shows that models struggle with unanswerable questions, supporting explicit evidence-sufficiency checks rather than relying on confident explanations.

Calibrate the rubric against the available twenty users’ feedback: inspect agreement and false-positive complaints by criterion and category, report abstention coverage, and examine disagreements with cited evidence. Keep rubric-development examples separate from evaluation where feasible; repeated recommendations from one user are correlated observations. Treat estimates as exploratory given five users per category. Detailed instructions alone offer limited assurance of judge validity, according to [Evaluating the Evaluator (2024/2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08781). These probes explain potential failures; the pinned macro validation HR@10 remains the model-selection metric.
